title: Altium Designer STM32 Test Board
summary: Designed a compact, custom STM32-based test board featuring USB-C power delivery, an onboard buck converter, and integrated motion sensing. The project was developed entirely in Altium Designer, utilizing hierarchical schematic design.
details: Structured a modular hardware design in Altium using top-level hierarchical block schematics for Power, Microcontroller, and Peripherals.
Engineered a power delivery system utilizing a USB-C connector and an LTC3405ES6 buck converter to step down +5V to a stable +3.3V.
Integrated an STM32F042G6U6 microcontroller running on a 24MHz external crystal oscillator.
Interfaced a high-performance BMI088 Inertial Measurement Unit (IMU) via SPI and provided an external I2C expansion header.
Optimized PCB footprint real estate by utilizing a zero-cost TC2030-IDC-NL "Tag-Connect" footprint for SWD programming and debugging.

sections.heading: Hierarchical Schematic Design
sections.body: The project utilizes a top-down hierarchical design methodology in Altium Designer to ensure clean, readable, and reusable schematics. The system is broken down into three primary modules: Power, Microcontroller, and Peripherals, making the netlist generation and team collaboration highly efficient.

sections.heading: Power Regulation Architecture
sections.body: Power is supplied via a modern USB4105-GF-A-060 USB-C connector. To power the logic components, an LTC3405ES6 synchronous step-down (buck) DC/DC converter is implemented with a 10uH inductor (NRH2412T100MNGH), efficiently stepping the +5V VBUS down to a clean +3.3V rail.

sections.heading: Microcontroller & Sensor Integration
sections.body: The core of the board is an STM32F042G6U6 ARM Cortex-M0 microcontroller paired with a 24MHz crystal (Y200) for precise timing. For spatial tracking and telemetry, the MCU interfaces with a BMI088 6-axis IMU over an SPI bus. Additionally, a 6-pin SM06B-SRSS-TB connector exposes the I2C bus for future peripheral expansion.

sections.heading: PCB Layout & 3D Modeling
sections.body: The physical layout was executed in Altium Designer with a focus on signal integrity and compact component placement. Care was taken to properly route the differential USB pairs and high-speed SPI traces. Altium's 3D visualization capabilities were utilized to verify component clearances, connector placement, and the physical manufacturing constraints of the final assembly.

title: UHF Satellite Image Transfer & SDR Antenna Testing
summary: Developed and validated an end-to-end Software-Defined Radio (SDR) communication link at 435 MHz to facilitate wireless image transfer. The project involved designing BPSK modulation pipelines in GNU Radio and developing custom Python telemetry scripts.
details: Designed transmit and receive flowgraphs in GNU Radio for 435 MHz UHF communication using HackRF and RTL-SDR hardware operating at 2 MS/s.
Implemented a BPSK demodulation pipeline featuring root-raised cosine (RRC) filtering, Costas loop carrier recovery, and differential decoding.
Developed an automated, multi-threaded Python monitoring script to parse incoming binary streams, lock onto frame headers (0xDEADBEEF), and extract payloads in real time.
Conducted physical antenna testing by calculating live link metrics, including Effective Data Rate (kbps) and Bit Error Rate (BER), to validate signal integrity.

sections.heading: SDR Transmit & Receive Architecture
sections.body: To test the ground station antenna's reception capabilities, a complete RF testing pipeline was established. The transmitter flowgraph was configured to broadcast data packets via a HackRF SDR, wrapping the payload with custom preamble and postamble markers. The receiver pipeline, powered by an RTL-SDR, handles the initial signal acquisition, down-conversion, and filtering to isolate the 435 MHz carrier.

sections.heading: Carrier Recovery & Demodulation
sections.body: Ensuring signal integrity over the wireless link required a robust digital signal processing chain. The receiver utilizes a Symbol Sync block for timing recovery, combined with a Costas Loop to achieve phase lock and carrier recovery. The BPSK constellation is then decoded, passed through a differential decoder, and verified against a CRC32 checksum to ensure the incoming packets are uncorrupted.

sections.heading: Automated Telemetry & BER Analysis
sections.body: To quantify the antenna's tracking efficiency, a custom Python monitor was embedded directly into the GNU Radio receiver. The script continuously scans the raw binary output for a specific magic byte sequence to identify frame boundaries. Upon detecting a complete frame, it automatically extracts the payload, saves the clean image file, and prints real-time Link and BER metrics to validate the accuracy of the RF transfer.

title: Adaptive PID Controller for Antenna Tracking System
summary: Designed and implemented a dual-axis antenna tracking system using an Arduino Uno, AS5600 magnetic rotary encoders, and a custom PID controller. The system drives high-inertia 12V wiper motors with built-in safety features.
details: Engineered a distributed I²C sensor architecture using a PCA9548A multiplexer and BTS7960 H-bridge drivers for bidirectional motor control.
Developed deterministic 50Hz control loop firmware with a custom ASCII command protocol, emergency stop, and 10-second stall timeout protections.
Achieved a 3.7-second settling time for 90° steps and an average steady-state tracking error of 0.6° under no-load conditions.

sections.heading: Hardware Architecture
sections.body: The tracking system relies on a distributed sensor architecture centered around an Arduino Uno. A PCA9548A I²C multiplexer was used to interface multiple AS5600 12-bit magnetic encoders, successfully eliminating address conflicts. BTS7960 H-bridge drivers provided the necessary high-current bidirectional control for the 12V permanent-magnet wiper motors.

sections.heading: Firmware & Control Logic
sections.body: The firmware executes two coordinated PID loops operating at a deterministic 50Hz (20ms) sampling rate. It communicates via a custom ASCII-based command protocol (e.g., AZ:90.5 EL:45.0). To protect the hardware, the software integrates strict safety mechanisms, including an immediate emergency stop, a 10-second stall timeout, and PWM output limiting to prevent over-current conditions.

sections.heading: PID Tuning & Experimental Results
sections.body: Classical Ziegler-Nichols autotuning failed due to motor non-linearities and mechanical friction, requiring a rigorous manual tuning methodology. Using a 6-step manual tuning process, the final PID gains were established at K_p=2.15, K_i=0.25, and K_d=0.2. Experimental trials demonstrated a maximum step overshoot of just 7.9% and stable sequential multi-target tracking without integrator wind-up.

title: 437 MHz 9-element long-Yagi
summary: Nine-element DL6WU long-Yagi for the 70 cm band, designed to feed 50 Ω directly with only a 1:1 balun, and documented as a full construction manual.
details: Designed a 9-element Rothammel/DL6WU long-Yagi for 437 MHz: 1283 mm round-boom array of one reflector, a straight half-wave dipole and seven directors, calculated for 11.24 dBd (13.39 dBi) over 428–446 MHz
Sized the driven element from theory rather than by trial: a 343 mm half-wave scaled by a 0.959 thickness-correction factor to two 164.6 mm halves across a 3.4 mm feed gap
Eliminated the matching network by choosing a straight dipole over a folded one, putting the feedpoint near 50 Ω so only a 1:1 balun is needed instead of an impedance step-up

Carried the boom diameter through the calculation as a design variable (d/λ = 0.007, D/λ = 0.015), so element lengths and the 51→216 mm progressive director spacing stay valid for the 10 mm round boom actually used

title: Five-phase IPMSM field-oriented control
summary: Dual-plane field-oriented control of a five-phase IPMSM, taken from an open-loop machine model to a closed-loop drive with five PID loops and five-phase SVPWM, then to ePWM on TI C2000 hardware.
details: Built a five-phase IPMSM model in Simulink with dual-plane Clarke/Park transforms, resolving the machine into a fundamental (d1-q1) and a third-harmonic (d3-q3) plane rather than the single plane a three-phase drive needs
Implemented torque production across both planes, including the reluctance term (Ld−Lq)·id·iq and the third-harmonic contribution, so injected third-harmonic current adds torque instead of only loss
Closed five control loops — one speed loop and four current loops — and tuned them with Simulink's Closed-Loop PID Autotuner against the plant model
Generated gate signals with five-phase space-vector PWM, driving a 10-switch two-level inverter at a 2 µs discrete step
Derived loss-aware MTPA with Lagrange multipliers and solved it numerically with Newton-Raphson, and implemented direct torque control with 20-sector hysteresis switching as a comparison scheme
Ported the modulator to a TI C2000 DSP in Code Composer Studio, generating ePWM and testing the gate driver circuit

sections.heading: The problem
sections.body:
A three-phase drive has one current plane and two degrees of freedom. A five-phase machine has two planes and four, and most of the extra freedom is usually thrown away — the third-harmonic plane is treated as a loss path to be suppressed rather than a place to make torque.

Five-phase machines are used where a lost phase must not stop the machine, so the control has to be built around that structure from the start rather than bolted on afterwards. The question I wanted to answer was what it actually takes to control both planes at once, and whether the second plane earns its complexity.

sections.heading: Approach
sections.body:
I built the drive in two stages rather than one.

The first model excites the machine open-loop with sinusoidal voltages and verifies the transforms and the electrical model in isolation — no controller, no modulator, nothing that could mask a modelling error. It runs at a 10 µs step because nothing in it switches.

Only once that was trustworthy did I close the loops. The second model adds the inverter, the modulator and five PID loops, and drops to a 2 µs step so the switching instants land on the grid properly. Separating the two meant that when the closed-loop model misbehaved I already knew the plant underneath it was right.

sections.heading: Key features
sections.body:
- Dual-plane decomposition: fundamental (d1-q1) and third-harmonic (d3-q3) planes controlled independently
- Five regulators: outer speed loop, four inner current loops
- Loss-aware MTPA using Lagrange multipliers, solved by Newton-Raphson
- Flux weakening limited by the available DC-link voltage
- Five-phase SVPWM modulator driving a 10-switch two-level inverter
- Direct torque control with 20-sector hysteresis switching, as a comparison
- Load-torque step disturbance for testing transient response

sections.heading: Technologies
sections.body: MATLAB and Simulink, Simscape Electrical (Specialized Power Systems), Stateflow for the transform and modulator logic, Simulink Control Design for autotuning, and Code Composer Studio for the DSP target.

sections.heading: Software components
sections.body: A five-phase coordinate transform block pair (forward and inverse) handling both planes. A torque computation implementing the dual-plane expression. Five discrete PID regulators. An MTPA solver. An SVPWM modulator plus a comparison modulation path. Stateflow charts carrying the abc-to-dq and dq-to-abc mappings.

sections.heading: Technical detail
sections.body:
The transform uses the standard 2/5 scaling with 72° phase separation, so the fundamental plane maps on cos/sin of θe and the third-harmonic plane on cos/sin of 3θe. Torque comes out as

Te = (5P/4)·[ λm·iq1 + (Ld1−Lq1)·id1·iq1 + 3λm3·iq3 + (Ld3−Lq3)·id3·iq3 ]

The first two terms are the familiar magnet and reluctance torque; the second pair is the third-harmonic plane's contribution, which is why injecting third-harmonic current raises torque rather than just heating the machine.

Because Lq1 > Ld1, the reluctance term is only positive for negative id1, which is what sets the MTPA trajectory. Solving MTPA with a loss term rather than pure copper-loss minimisation has no closed form, hence the Newton-Raphson solver.

The closed-loop model runs fixed-step discrete at 2 µs. The switching period has to be an exact multiple of the step or the modulator jitters, which shows up as current ripple that looks like a tuning problem and isn't.

sections.heading: My contribution
sections.body:
I did the mathematical modelling and the simulation design. Professor Saifullah Payami and PhD scholar Amitesh Kumar provided a reference paper and a working three-phase reference model as the starting point.

Extending that to five phases was mine. A three-phase machine has one current plane; a five-phase machine has two, so the transform is not a matter of adding two more columns. I derived the five-phase Clarke and Park transforms myself — the fundamental plane on 72° spacing and the third-harmonic plane on 3θe, both with the 2/5 scaling — along with the dual-plane torque expression and the structure of the five regulators that sit on top of it.

sections.heading: Results
sections.body:
The closed-loop drive was run against a 1500 rpm (157 rad/s) speed reference with a 10 N·m load torque applied as a step at t = 5 s.

Speed reaches the 157 rad/s reference in about 0.2 s, with roughly 3.8% overshoot (peak ≈163 rad/s) and no steady-state error.
The load step produces no visible speed deviation at plot scale — the speed loop rejects it faster than the trace resolves.
Electromagnetic torque settles exactly on the 10 N·m load, after ≈32 N·m during acceleration.
q-axis current tracks torque demand: 15 A accelerating, ≈0 A unloaded, 4.7 A holding 10 N·m. Both figures give the same 2.13 N·m/A, which confirms the torque expression and the transform agree with each other.
d-axis current is held at zero throughout, and the third-harmonic plane currents stay within about ±0.9 A, so the second plane carries ripple only and no net current.

title: Two-axis satellite antenna tracker
summary: Azimuth–elevation tracker for UHF satellite passes, built end to end at Orbitalink.
details: Fusion 360 chassis optimised for rigidity and low weight
NEMA23 hybrid servos on HSD57 drivers with trapezoidal motion ramps
EEPROM-saved parameters and a serial command protocol
Now porting to STM32F411 as modular firmware

title: 435 MHz cross-Yagi antenna
summary: Circularly polarised 14-element cross-Yagi for 435 MHz satellite work, phased mechanically by a quarter-wavelength boom offset and matched to 50 Ω with quarter-wave transformers.
details: Designed a 14-element cross-Yagi for 435 MHz — two orthogonal 7-element arrays (reflector, driven element, five directors) on a shared 1.14 m boom, modelled wire-by-wire in MMANA-GAL

Achieved circular polarisation by mechanical phasing: offsetting the vertical plane 172.3 mm (a free-space quarter wavelength) along the boom, so both driven elements are fed in phase with no delay line to build or tune

Solved the 50 Ω match with a quarter-wave transformer pair — two 36 Ω antennas paralleled directly give 18 Ω and 2.8:1 SWR, so each is fed through a quarter wavelength of 60 Ω line to present 100 Ω, and the two in parallel land on 50 Ω
Built the full 14-wire geometry in MMANA-GAL with two independent sources, and swept the pattern over real ground at 3 m to get realistic take-off angle and gain figures

sections.heading: The Problem
sections.body:
Satellites tumble, and their antennas point wherever the spacecraft happens to be pointing. A linearly polarised ground antenna therefore suffers deep, unpredictable fades as the polarisation of the arriving signal rotates against it — losses that can exceed 20 dB at the worst alignment.

Circular polarisation removes that failure mode: a circularly polarised antenna accepts either linear orientation at a constant 3 dB penalty rather than an occasional total null. The cost is that you now need two antennas, fed 90° out of phase, and something to combine them without wrecking the match.

sections.heading: Approach
sections.body:
Two orthogonal Yagis on one boom, with the phase quadrature produced by geometry rather than by electronics.

Instead of building a phasing harness with an electrical quarter-wave delay line, I offset the entire vertical-plane array 172.3 mm along the boom — one free-space quarter wavelength at 435 MHz. The wavefront reaches the two driven elements a quarter cycle apart, so feeding both in phase produces circular polarisation. There is no delay line to cut, no velocity factor to get wrong, and nothing that drifts.

That decision moved the hard part into the matching network, which I solved separately with quarter-wave transformers.

sections.heading: Key features
sections.body:
- 14 elements: two orthogonal 7-element arrays on a shared 35 mm square boom
- Mechanical phasing — 172.3 mm boom offset in place of an electrical delay line
- Both driven elements fed at 0° phase, simplifying the harness to two equal cables
- Quarter-wave 60 Ω transformers converting 36 Ω per antenna to 100 Ω, paralleling to 50 Ω
- Element lengths tapering 319.3 mm (reflector) to 278.3 mm (last director)
- Modelled over real ground at 3 m to give a usable take-off angle rather than a free-space figure

sections.heading: Technologies
sections.body: MMANA-GAL (NEC-2 method-of-moments), transmission-line theory for the matching network, and hand calculation for the phasing geometry.

sections.heading: Hardware
sections.body: 35 × 35 mm square aluminium boom, roughly 1.16–1.17 m of stock for a 1.14 m active length. Aluminium tube elements on insulated standoffs. Feed: two equal quarter-wave sections of 60 Ω coaxial line into a parallel junction, then 50 Ω coax to the SDR.

sections.heading: Software components
sections.body: A 14-wire MMANA-GAL model with two independent sources (wire 2 for the horizontal plane, wire 9 for the vertical), 9 segments per element, auto-segmentation at DM1 200 / DM2 20, and a real-ground environment at 3 m height.

sections.heading: Technical detail
sections.body:
Phasing. At 435 MHz, λ = 689.1 mm, so a quarter wavelength in free space is 172.3 mm. Offsetting the vertical array by exactly that distance along the boom gives the 90° spatial phase difference circular polarisation requires. Every vertical-plane element therefore sits at its horizontal-plane counterpart's position plus 172.3 mm — reflector at 172.3 mm, driven at 351.8 mm, and so on to the last director at 1140 mm.

Matching. Each array presents approximately 36 Ω resistive at resonance. Two of those in parallel give 18 Ω, which against 50 Ω coax is a 2.8:1 SWR — roughly 23% of forward power reflected. A quarter-wave transformer converts an impedance by Zin = Z0²/ZL, so choosing Z0 = √(36 × 100) = 60 Ω turns each 36 Ω feedpoint into 100 Ω. Two 100 Ω sources in parallel present 50 Ω, and the SWR collapses to near unity.

The transformer sections must be an ELECTRICAL quarter wavelength, so the physical length is 172.3 mm × the cable's velocity factor — about 114 mm for solid polyethylene at VF 0.66, or 141 mm for foam at 0.82. Cutting them to the free-space 172.3 mm is the single most common way to get this wrong, and it detunes the match completely.

sections.heading: My contribution
sections.body: I did the antenna design: the element lengths and spacings, the decision to phase mechanically rather than electrically, the MMANA-GAL model and its sweeps, and the quarter-wave transformer matching network. Work carried out at Orbitalink for the satellite ground station.

sections.heading: Results
sections.body:
Modelled performance at 435 MHz over real ground at 3 m height: 16.67 dBi gain (this figure includes ground reflection gain; free-space gain is substantially lower), 13.19 dB front-to-back ratio, and a 3.2° take-off angle suited to low-elevation satellite passes.

The current model reports a driven-element impedance of 30.22 − j35.51 Ω. The reactive part shows the driven elements are still electrically short at 435 MHz, so the array is not yet resonant and the quarter-wave match — which assumes a resistive 36 Ω — cannot be applied until that is tuned out.

Not yet built or measured. Next step is trimming to resonance, then a VNA sweep of the assembled array.

title: DC-DC boost converter
summary: Simulink model analysing steady-state and transient response across duty cycles and loads.
details: Open-loop boost converter modelled in Simscape Electrical: 20 V input, 10 kHz switching at 50% duty, 3.5 mH inductor and 572 µF output capacitor into a 200 Ω load
Measured 39.2 V output against the ideal Vin/(1−D) = 40 V, tracing the shortfall to the 0.8 V diode drop and the MOSFET's 0.1 Ω on-resistance
Verified continuous conduction mode: critical inductance is 1.25 mH, so the 3.5 mH choke holds inductor ripple to 0.29 A peak-to-peak on a 0.39 A average
Instrumented inductor, switch, diode and capacitor currents alongside inductor, switch and load voltages, with a Mean block averaging output voltage over one switching period

Diagnosed a startup failure mode: a lightly damped L-C pair (Q ≈ 40) driven by a hard duty step produced a 15 A inductor peak and 74 V output overshoot, both well beyond the ratings a 40 V, 0.4 A design would use
Fixed it by pre-charging the output capacitor to Vin and ramping duty from 0 to 0.5 over 100 ms through a PWM Generator, cutting the peak to 0.9 A and 40.1 V — a 17× reduction in inrush current

title: Weather dashboard
summary: Responsive app with live weather for any city and API error handling, deployed on Render.
details: Server-rendered Node/Express app with a POST route that queries the OpenWeatherMap current-weather API for any city
Renders seven live readings per lookup: temperature, humidity, visibility, wind speed, cloudiness, sunrise and sunset
Bootstrap offcanvas navigation and a mobile-first layout that collapses to a single column on phones
Unknown or misspelled city names return to the search form instead of throwing, so a bad lookup never crashes the server
Deployed on Render with the API key held in an environment variable rather than committed to the repository
